exp20v2-val.experiments:
Designing discovery experiments

Discovery & Design › Discovery & Assumption Testing. The question: what is the cheapest test that could prove this assumption wrong?

1. A Monday in Nashik

On Monday, 9 March 2026, Kaveh Mandalia, head of product at Udbhav Fresh Logistics, had a six-month plan on his screen and a board meeting on 27 March at which it would be approved or not. Udbhav ran cold rooms in the grape and pomegranate belt around Nashik and rented space by the crate to fruit traders. The plan was a product called Ulaas: a mobile app through which a trader could reserve a cold-room slot for the following season, pay a deposit by UPI, and see the room's temperature log from the mandi. Building it would take a team of five for six months at roughly ₹8 lakh a month, a total of ₹48 lakh. Kaustav Manjrekar, who ran operations, wanted it; two large traders had mentioned it to him over tea.

Kaveh did not doubt that Ulaas could be built. His doubt was narrower and, he suspected, more expensive. The plan assumed that enough of Udbhav's roughly 5,000 registered traders would pay in advance, through an app, for something they currently arranged by phone call and a handshake. If perhaps one in twenty did, the product would be a handsome piece of software that nobody needed.

The choice before him was not "build or do not build". It was the choice of what to do in the next week, before the board met, that could most cheaply show the plan to be wrong. This page is about how that choice is made. It follows Kaveh through it and uses his numbers throughout, so that each idea is attached to a decision with a price.

2. The idea

A discovery experiment is a deliberately small, time-boxed test, run before a product is built, designed so that one specific assumption about customers, technology or economics can fail in public. An assumption is a belief the plan depends on and for which the team has no direct evidence yet. A hypothesis is the same belief written so that it can be checked: it names who does what, how many, by when.

The idea grew out of three bodies of work. Steve Blank's customer development, from the early 2000s, told founders to leave the building and test their guesses against customers before scaling. Eric Ries, in The Lean Startup (2011), turned this into the build-measure-learn loop and the "minimum viable product". Alberto Savoia, a Google engineer, argued in his work on "pretotyping" around the same years that one should first test whether people would use something before testing whether one can build it. David Bland and Alexander Osterwalder's Testing Business Ideas (2019) and Teresa Torres's Continuous Discovery Habits (2021) added the working vocabulary used here: map your assumptions, rank them, and match each to a test.

Kaveh's sentence for the meeting: “For each belief this plan rests on, we should run the cheapest test that could prove it wrong, and we should decide in advance what result would make us stop.”

The sentence does not say “validate the idea”. A test built to confirm almost always succeeds; only a test built to disprove means anything when it passes.

3. How it works

The procedure has five steps, and the third and fifth are the ones practitioners tend to skip. Kaveh's afternoon with Kaustav and two engineers, ran through them in order.

Step one: list the assumptions. The plan was turned into plain sentences. Traders will reserve in advance. Traders will pay a deposit through UPI. A temperature log on a phone matters to them. Udbhav's sensors can feed the app reliably. Reservations will leave rooms fuller, not merely shuffle the same bookings earlier. Marty Cagan's four product risks give a check on completeness: value (will they want it), usability (can they work it), feasibility (can we build it) and viability (does the business work). The list had to touch all four.

Step two: rank by importance and by how little is known. Importance means: if this assumption is false, does the plan collapse? Evidence means: what do we already have that is better than opinion? The assumptions that are both critical and unevidenced come first. Figure 1 shows how Kaveh's six fell, F being the usability assumption: that a trader can complete a UPI booking on a phone, at the mandi, in a crowd.

The map is a judgement, and it was argued over. Kaustav wanted D, the temperature log, placed higher; Kaveh noted that two traders asking over tea was weak evidence.

Step three: write the kill criterion before the test. This is the step most often left implicit. A kill criterion is the result, fixed in advance, below which the team will stop, change course or test again. Without one, any result can be read as encouraging: a 5 per cent response can be called “a promising start” or “a weak signal” according to the mood of the room. Kaveh derived his from the plan's own economics, shown in the next section.

Step four: choose the cheapest test that can fail. A test has two properties that pull against each other: its cost, in money and calendar days, and its strength, meaning how closely the behaviour it observes resembles the behaviour the real product depends on. Opinions in an interview are cheap and weak; a customer handing over money is dearer and strong. The craft is choosing the cheapest rung that is still strong enough to embarrass the assumption. Figure 2 is the ladder Kaveh used.

Test (rung)Assumption it can attackCost (₹ lakh)Elapsed
Eight trader interviewsA, D (stated intent)0.25 days
Fake door: WhatsApp offer with ₹500 refundable depositA, B, F (paid intent; 22 paid by UPI)0.56 days
Concierge pilot: 12 traders, bookings by hand, weekly crates measuredA, E and contribution per trader3.05 weeks
Build Ulaas (five people, six months at ₹8 lakh)All, at once48.06 months

Table 1. Cost of each rung for Udbhav; the build row is 6 × 8 = 48. The fake door costs about 1 per cent of the build (0.5 against 48, a ratio of 96 to 1).

A fake door (also called a painted door) is an offer for a feature that does not yet exist; the customer who walks through it meets a polite message instead of a product. A concierge test delivers the service by hand, with people doing behind the curtain what software will eventually do, so the customer experiences the value before any code exists.

Step five: decide what each outcome will cause. The last step is the one that makes the experiment a decision tool rather than a research exercise. For each possible result the team writes the action that follows: build, redesign, test again, or stop. If a result would change nothing, the test is not worth its cost.

4. A worked example, line by line

Deriving the kill criterion. Kaveh started from what the plan needed in order to pay back. The build costs ₹48 lakh, which is ₹4,800,000. He wanted payback within two years. A trader who adopted Ulaas would generate contribution, meaning revenue less the direct cost of serving them, from the extra crates stored. Kaustav's estimate, from the rooms' booking history, was 24 crates a week for a 25-week season at a margin of ₹10 a crate: 24 × 25 × 10 = ₹6,000 per trader per year. Over two years that is ₹12,000. The number of adopting traders needed is therefore 4,800,000 ÷ 12,000 = 400. Against a base of 5,000 registered traders, 400 is 8 per cent. So: if fewer than about 8 per cent of traders will commit, the plan does not pay back in two years.

The test. On Wednesday, 11 March, Udbhav sent a WhatsApp message to 400 traders drawn at random from the 5,000-trader list, offering a reserved slot for the November season in return for a ₹500 deposit by UPI, refundable until 31 August. All 400 messages showed as delivered. Delivery was the denominator, not the number who opened the message, because the 8 per cent threshold is a share of the whole list, and traders who ignore a message would also ignore an app. The offer closed on Tuesday, 17 March. Twenty-two traders paid. Total deposits were 22 × ₹500 = ₹11,000, all of it refundable.

Reading the result. The rate is 22 ÷ 400 = 5.5 per cent. That is below 8, but a rate from 400 people is an estimate with a margin around it. The standard way to express the margin for a proportion is a 95 per cent confidence interval, the range that would contain the true rate in 95 out of 100 repeats of the same procedure. Using the Wilson method, which behaves well for modest counts, 22 of 400 gives an interval of 3.7 to 8.2 per cent. The upper end, 8.2, is above the 8 per cent threshold. The honest reading is not “we have failed” but “we cannot yet rule out that the plan clears the bar, and we cannot say it does”. Table 2 lists the cells behind every interval in this section.

PassDeposits (k)Traders reached (n)Rate k/n95% Wilson interval
Wave 1, 11–17 March224005.50%3.66% to 8.19%
Wave 2, 24–30 March (a fresh 400)194004.75%3.06% to 7.30%
Both waves pooled418005.13%3.80% to 6.88%

Table 2. Counts and intervals for the Ulaas fake door. Pooled row: 22 + 19 = 41 and 400 + 400 = 800. The waves used non-overlapping random draws from the same 5,000-trader list.

The second pass: one input changes. Because Wave 1 straddled the line, Kaveh did not build; he spent another ₹0.5 lakh on a second, independent wave. It returned 19 of 400, or 4.75 per cent. Pooling the two (41 of 800, or 5.13 per cent) narrows the interval from about 4.5 points wide to about 3.1, and moves the upper end to 6.88. Against the 8 per cent bar the plan now fails: even the optimistic end of the range is below the threshold. (Wave 2 was commissioned because wave 1 was ambiguous, so pooling after that decision is a mild sequential-testing problem and the pooled interval is slightly generous.)

Now change a different input, the contribution per trader. Suppose Kaustav is wrong about volumes and a typical adopter moves 30 crates a week, not 24: 30 × 25 × 10 = ₹7,500 a year, ₹15,000 over two years. Required adopters become 4,800,000 ÷ 15,000 = 320, which is 6.4 per cent of 5,000. The pooled interval, 3.80 to 6.88, contains 6.4. The experiment then cannot decide the matter, and the uncertainty has moved from demand to economics. The recommendation survives either way: do not commit ₹48 lakh yet, because under the base case the plan fails and under the generous case it is unresolved. But the next test changes: it should attack contribution per trader, which is exactly what a concierge pilot measures.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Cheapest does not mean weakest

Eight friendly interviews are cheaper than the fake door, but traders who say “sounds useful” pay nothing, and the assumption survives them whether true or false. A test that cannot fail is not cheap; it is wasted.

Say versus do

Stated intent systematically overstates behaviour. A ₹500 deposit is a small cost, yet it filters out most of the politeness. The more a test asks the customer to give up, the more the result resembles real behaviour.

A rate is an estimate, not a fact

The 5.5 per cent from Wave 1 was a single draw. Before running a test, ask how many responses you would need to separate the threshold from a clearly too-low result; if you cannot afford that many, choose a different question or rung.

Independence is assumed

The interval treats each trader as an independent draw. Traders in one mandi talk to and copy each other, which widens the true uncertainty, while sampling 800 of 5,000 (16 per cent) without replacement narrows it by about 8 per cent; the two effects pull in opposite directions and we have not quantified the net. The draw also speaks only for Udbhav's registered traders, the same list on which the 8 per cent bar was computed.

A deposit rate is not an adoption rate

Paying ₹500 once says less than booking and using a slot in November. The deposit rate is, if anything, an upper bound on adoption, since some payers may never use the app. That strengthens "do not build" and weakens any reading of a pass.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

In consumer products, volume is cheap and the problem is the weakness of the signal: a tap is not a commitment, so teams climb quickly to a payment or repeat visit. In B2B products, like Ulaas, there are few buyers, each decision involves several people, and the sample is small. Tests lean on conversations, letters of intent, deposits and hand-delivered pilots, and a single enterprise “yes” carries more weight than a thousand clicks. In a marketplace, two sides must be tested, and the assumption that kills most marketplaces is on the scarcer side: will enough supply show up to make demand worth coming for?

Company size matters too. A start-up can treat the build as its final experiment; a large company's danger is process, so mature teams pre-agree a budget and approver for small tests.

7. Common mistakes

Testing the easy assumption. Symptom: the team reports a strong result on something nobody doubted, for example that traders find the temperature log interesting, while the deposit question is untouched. Misunderstanding: choosing tests by convenience rather than by importance and absence of evidence. Diagnostic: ask which assumption on the map the test attacks, and whether the plan survives if the answer is no.

Setting the bar after the result. Symptom: a 5.5 per cent response is described as “encouraging” by one person and “disappointing” by another. Misunderstanding: the threshold lives in people's heads. Diagnostic: find the document, dated before launch, that states what result leads to what action. If there is none, there was no experiment.

Confusing a signal with a sample. Symptom: a decision made on 8 conversations or on two enthusiastic letters, quoted as “25 per cent interest”. Two of eight has an interval from about 7 to 59 per cent. Diagnostic: ask for the numerator and the denominator, and compute the interval.

8. What good looks like

Seen from the outside, the strong version of Kaveh's week has a recognisable shape. On Monday there is a one-page list of assumptions, ranked, with the two riskiest marked. By Tuesday each has a test, a cost and a written kill criterion derived from the plan's own economics. By Wednesday the cheapest test is live, for about ₹50,000, and the board knows in advance which results lead to which decisions. When the first result is ambiguous, the team spends a little more to narrow the interval instead of arguing about interpretation. The person who proposed Ulaas helps write the criteria for its failure; that is the clearest sign the culture is working.

9. What Kaveh decided

On 27 March the board saw Wave 1 and was told that Wave 2 would report on 30 March. It deferred the build. On 31 March Kaveh reported the pooled result and recommended against committing ₹48 lakh. His reasoning had three parts. Under the base economics the plan needed 8 per cent of traders and the evidence pointed to about 5; the best case of the data, 6.9 per cent, was still short. Only contribution per trader, unmeasured, could rescue it, and the concierge pilot that measures it cost ₹3.0 lakh, about 6 per cent of the build. The board approved a five-week pilot in April and May with twelve traders, measuring average crates a week per trader. The criterion was a rule, not one number. Required crates a week equal 9,600 ÷ N, where N is the number of adopters: 4,800,000 ÷ (2 × N × 25 weeks × ₹10) simplifies to 9,600 ÷ N. At N = 344, the top of the pooled interval, that is 27.9; at 320, 30; at 256, 37.5. The board agreed: below 28 crates, shelve Ulaas, because it fails even on the best case of the data; at 38 or more, build, because it works on the point estimate; between the two, the pilot has not decided and adoption must be measured before any build. Deposit payers are not adopters, so true N is probably below 256 and 38 is, if anything, lenient; it is also 58 per cent above Kaustav's 24-crate estimate, so shelving was the likely outcome, and Kaveh said so.

Kaveh's summary to a disappointed Kaustav: Ulaas had not been shown to be a bad idea, only to have not yet earned its budget.

What to learn next. Read about fake doors and landing-page smoke tests, then concierge and Wizard of Oz tests, because they are the two cheapest rungs in practice. Then study kill criteria and decision rules, and the evidence ladder.

Two questions to sit with.

1. Think of a plan you are now supporting. Which single assumption, if false, would sink it, and what is the cheapest thing you could do this week that might show it false? 2. Suppose Kaveh's Wave 1 had returned 32 of 400, exactly 8.0 per cent, with an interval of 5.7 to 11.1 per cent. What would you have wanted written down, before the test, to decide whether that justified a build?
case20v1-val.experiments:
Anaaj Ghar: Credit for the Corner Store

A teaching case on designing discovery experiments

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday 19 October 2026, Ishita Phatak, chief product officer of Anaaj Ghar Technologies, sat in the company's Baner office in Pune with a single slide due for the board on Friday 23 October. The slide had to answer one question: what should Anaaj Ghar do about offering credit to the kirana stores that buy their groceries through its app?

The chief executive, Ishan Prabhudesai, had already said what he wanted. He wanted a build approved at ₹1.8 crore, with credit live "as soon as engineering can manage". Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, the heaviest stocking season of a store owner's year, and he did not want the company absent. Ishita was not sure the company knew enough to spend that money.

2. Company background

Anaaj Ghar, founded in Pune in 2021, lets a kirana owner order rice, atta, oil, pulses and packaged goods from partner wholesalers for next-morning delivery. It earns a take rate of 2.4 per cent on goods value. In September 2026, 11,400 stores had ordered at least once in the previous thirty days, spread across Pune, Nashik, Kolhapur, Nagpur and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. They bought about ₹85.5 crore a month, an average of ₹75,000 per active store, which gave the company net revenue of roughly ₹2.05 crore a month.

The business was concentrated. The 6,840 stores that ordered three or more times a month, 60 per cent of the base, bought about ₹1,10,000 each, or ₹75.24 crore in all, 88 per cent of the GMV. The other 4,560 bought ₹22,500 each.

Udaan, Jumbotail and JioMart Partner all sold to the same owners, and Khatabook and OkCredit already held the ledger relationship with many stores. Anaaj Ghar had raised ₹140 crore in total and held about ₹62 crore in cash, so the proposed ₹1.8 crore was 2.9 per cent of cash.

3. The situation

Informal udhaar from a local distributor is how many kiranas finance the weeks before a festival. In August, Ishita's team interviewed 48 owners in Pune and Nashik, all drawn from the 6,840 frequent stores, and asked whether they would use credit from Anaaj Ghar. Exhibit 1 shows the result: 31 said yes. The yes answers cluster among owners who already buy on udhaar, and no interviewee was quoted a price.

Exhibit 1. Stated interest in Anaaj Ghar credit, August 2026 interviews

Total / average483164.6

Interviewees: 26 in Pune, 22 in Nashik. The last row is a pooled rate (31 of 48), not a mean of the two rates. Stated intent, not behaviour.

The global team read the picture differently. Indumati Puranik, the data scientist in Toronto, joined a Friday 16 October call at 7:30 a.m. her time (5:00 p.m. in Pune) and warned that nobody had repayment data: "We would be pricing a loan book we have never seen." Ivan Patkar, who runs the support desk from Singapore (7:30 p.m.), reported that in September 212 support tickets mentioned credit or udhaar, but they came from only 163 distinct stores, 1.4 per cent of the 11,400 active stores. Ilina Pai, the designer in Berlin (1:30 p.m.), had tested a credit-checkout prototype with eight owners; seven completed it unaided.

A partner non-banking lender would have to approve limits under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions, and order data could be shared with it only with consent under the DPDP Act. Two NBFCs had shown interest; neither had signed. Counsel had also advised that a 14-day deferred-payment term on Anaaj Ghar's own invoices counts as trade credit, whereas passing on lender money would not.

4. The people

Ishan Prabhudesai, chief executive and co-founder, Pune, wants speed. He points to stated interest among nearly two in three of the 48 frequent-store owners interviewed.

Ishita Phatak, chief product officer, Pune, must carry a recommendation to the board and be able to defend it.

Indumati Puranik, data scientist, Toronto, wants evidence about repayment before any capital is committed, and doubts that a small pilot can say anything about losses.

Ivan Patkar, customer-success lead, Singapore, fears that a half-working credit feature will flood his desk.

5. The economics and the assumptions

The proposed product gave a store a limit of up to ₹50,000, repayable in 14 days, for a fee of 1.5 per cent per cycle (about 39 per cent a year, simple). Per ₹100 of credit disbursed in a cycle, the fee brought ₹1.50. A partner lender would charge 12 per cent a year for funds, which is ₹0.46 for 14 days (12% × 14/365), servicing cost ₹0.20, leaving ₹0.84 before losses. The product only made money if losses stayed below 0.84 per cent of credit disbursed in each cycle.

If one in four frequent stores took credit, that was 1,710 stores. At an average ₹40,000 used per cycle, disbursals would be ₹6.84 crore a cycle, a contribution of about ₹5.75 lakh before losses, and, if every one of them borrowed every cycle, across 26 cycles roughly ₹1.49 crore a year, an upper case. The build cost ₹1.8 crore, made up of engineering ₹96 lakh, lender integration and legal ₹24 lakh, risk modelling ₹30 lakh and launch marketing ₹30 lakh.

Ishita restated the plan as four assumptions, one per product risk (Exhibit 2).

Exhibit 2. The credit plan as four testable assumptions

UsabilityAn owner can place a credit order unaided7 of 8 prototype testers did
FeasibilityA partner NBFC approves limits within one working day, lawfullyInterest from two NBFCs; no term sheet
ViabilityLosses stay below 0.84% of credit disbursed per cycleNone; Anaaj Ghar has never lent

6. The options

Option A: build the credit line now. Five months of work, finishing in late March 2027, would miss this Diwali. It would settle all four assumptions at once, but only after ₹1.8 crore was spent.

Option B: run a concierge pilot. Sixty frequent stores, twelve drawn at random from each of the five cities, would be offered the real product for eight weeks, 26 October to 20 December. Anaaj Ghar's own team would approve limits of ₹50,000 on a spreadsheet and collect repayments by UPI. Operations would cost ₹9 lakh, and the credit ceiling is 60 × ₹50,000 = ₹30 lakh, so cash at risk is at most ₹39 lakh, since a defaulter gets no new limit. Credit taken on Monday 26 October falls due on Monday 9 November (Figure 2).

Option C: put a fake door in the app. For ten days a "Pay in 14 days" button, with the 1.5 per cent fee shown, would appear at checkout for all stores. A tap would open a waitlist page. It costs ₹2.5 lakh and measures clicks, not repayment.

Exhibit 3. The three options compared

Option B's ₹30 lakh is a ceiling on outstanding credit, recoverable if repaid; it holds because a defaulting store gets no new limit. Credit taken in cycle 4 falls due between 21 Dec and 3 Jan, so repayment monitoring runs past the bar in Figure 2.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Which of the four assumptions in Exhibit 2 is the riskiest, and what in the case supports your ranking?

2. Exhibit 1 reports 64.6 per cent. Which owners does that figure represent, what were they not asked, and what would it take to turn stated interest into evidence?

3. For each option, what result would make Ishita abandon or reshape the credit plan, and can that option actually produce that result?

4. Which option would you take to the board, and what stop rules would you write down before it starts?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames the decision as matching: find the assumption that would hurt most if wrong, then choose the cheapest test that could prove it wrong. A good answer ranks the four risks, rejects tests that cannot fail, and fixes the pass-or-fail line before collecting data.

One defensible path is Option B. The interviews measured stated interest at no quoted price, so value is unproven. Usability and feasibility are tolerable risks, but viability has no evidence at all, and only lending real money can create it. Option C is cheaper but a tap costs a store nothing and says nothing about repayment. Option A buys every answer at ₹1.8 crore and arrives after Diwali.

The test should carry written rules. Stop if fewer than 15 of the 60 stores (25 per cent) use credit in at least two of the four cycles. Pause if more than 6 (10 per cent) pay over seven days late on any due date. Cycle 1 contains the Diwali stock-up, so it should be reported separately, which is why the value rule counts two cycles and not one.

The pilot also has limits. Sixty stores over four cycles cannot certify a loss rate of 0.84 per cent. They can only show warning signs, so a pass justifies a larger lender-backed pilot, not the full build. The 64.6 per cent (intent among 48 interviewees) and the 1.4 per cent (stores raising credit or udhaar tickets, as a share of all 11,400; the case does not split them by order frequency) measure different things, and neither shows demand at a 1.5 per cent fee.

Beriz Retail Technologies: Four Months of Evidence

An ambiguous decision case. Pune, November 2026.

1. Sunday night in Kharadi

On Sunday 15 November 2026, a little after eleven, Jui Rahalkar sat on the floor of her flat in Kharadi, Pune, with seven printed exhibits around her and a laptop open on a slide headed FY28 New Revenue Line. The slide was otherwise empty.

Rahalkar had been vice-president of product at Beriz Retail Technologies for five years. The board met on Friday 20 November; the pack closed Monday morning. Her chief executive, Jayant Raorane, had told her on 9 November that he would ask the board to approve a lending product, and expected her slide to say so. Her data scientist in Toronto had sent, at 2.14 that morning Pune time, a note headed none of these tested anything.

Between 1 June and 31 October the company had spent ₹47 lakh of a ₹1.60 crore discovery budget on eight pieces of work, and could not say what any of them had ruled out. Three candidate products were on the table; the money would fund one of them.

2. The company, and a cheque that still constrains it

Beriz was founded in Pune in 2017 by Raorane and two engineers who had written billing software for distributors. Beriz Counter runs the front counter of an independent chemist's shop: billing, GST e-invoicing, stock, expiry tracking and the Schedule H1 register the Drugs Rules require for certain antibiotics.

On 30 September 2026 Beriz had 10,240 live stores, of which 9,480 paid and 760 sat on a legacy free tier, at a blended ₹1,150 a month per paying store: ₹1.09 crore of monthly recurring revenue, ₹13.08 crore annualised. Cash was ₹18.4 crore against a ₹92 lakh net monthly burn, twenty months. Of 146 staff, 97 sat in Pune and 32 in Bengaluru; the other 17 were in Singapore, New Jersey, Dubai, Berlin and Toronto.

In March 2023 Beriz raised ₹22 crore, six of it from Bhimthadi Pharma Distribution, a distributor serving some 31,000 chemists in Maharashtra and Gujarat. The money brought a clause: until 31 March 2027 Beriz will not sell any feature that places a purchase order with a distributor to a store Bhimthadi does not serve in those two states. Bhimthadi also took a board observer seat. By 2026, 6,420 of the 10,240 live stores sat in those states, and the obvious adjacency — letting a chemist order stock from the screen he already uses — was the one thing Beriz could not sell.

3. The industry

India has an estimated nine lakh retail pharmacy outlets, most of them single-store businesses. Tata 1mg, PharmEasy, Netmeds and Apollo Pharmacy have changed what a patient expects of price and delivery, but the neighbourhood chemist still fills most chronic prescriptions in most of the country.

Four regulatory facts bear on what Beriz can sell. Retail pharmacy is licensed by state drug controllers under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, and the Schedule H1 register Beriz automates is a statutory obligation, which is most of why stores stay. Prices of scheduled formulations are capped by the NPPA, so a chemist's margin on exactly the chronic medicines a refill product would chase is thin and fixed. Anything touching a prescription handles sensitive data, and under the DPDP Act, 2023 the consent must be the patient's, not the pharmacist's. And credit would make Beriz a lending service provider under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions: it may source and service, but not lend.

Beriz is also an exporter. Jeevan Redkar runs enterprise and international sales from Edison, New Jersey, incorporated there in 2024. In July 2026 Baniyas Care Pharmacies of Dubai — 61 stores, run by a group pharmacy director named Jamshed Rasam — signed a memorandum worth about ₹2.10 crore over three years, conditional on a refill module live by 1 April 2027: about ₹9,600 a store a month, more than eight times the ₹1,150 blended India price.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The idea began in January 2026 with an observation from Joshna Rakshe in Singapore: a recurring ticket in which a chemist asked whether Beriz could tell him when a chronic patient was due back. In April the board approved the ₹1.60 crore budget and asked, in one line of the minutes, for “one new revenue line by FY28”. Nobody defined what counted. Eight pieces of work followed, dated in Exhibit 1 and costed in Exhibit 2.

In June a clickable prototype went to twelve owners in Pune and Nashik; nine said they would pay ₹400 a month. In July a “Refill (coming soon)” item was placed in the main menu, directly above Reports. In three weeks 1,860 of the 9,480 paying stores tapped it, 19.6 per cent, and 1,204 joined a waitlist. When that waitlist was called in October, 86 of the 1,204 answered, 7.1 per cent, and thirty-one of those 86 could say what they had signed up for.

Then the base came into question: a refill product needs the store to have recorded who the patient is. Rakshe's dashboard reported that 61 per cent of stores used the patient-record field; Rivonkar, querying the warehouse from Toronto, got 38 per cent. Both were right about different things, and a third definition gave 17 per cent (Exhibit 3).

Designing discovery experiments

Discovery & Design › Discovery & Assumption Testing — near-expert treatment. The question: what is the cheapest test that could prove this assumption wrong?

1. Two decisions, four weeks apart

On Friday 13 November 2026, Lavina Nadgir, chief product officer of Ujjayan Systems in Pune, had seven days before a roadmap commitment. Ujjayan sold order-promising software to mid-market discrete manufacturers — pump makers, forging shops, ACMA-member component suppliers. The proposal was Urmi Promise: a machine-learned committed-delivery-date engine to replace the planner's fixed buffer, at nine engineers for seven months plus a year of inference. Her chief executive wanted a number for the board. Lavina wanted a result that could prove the plan wrong before the money was spent.

Four weeks later, on Friday 11 December, Lochan Narvekar, vice-president of product at Ujas Care Networks in Bengaluru, faced a decision of a different shape. Ujas Care ran chronic-care programmes through 240 partner clinics, paid by an insurer for every patient-quarter in which the patient stayed on medicine. Urvaan added a loaned cuff, an app and two nurse calls a quarter; rolling it to 120 clinics would cost ₹210.00 lakh. Lochan had already spent ₹41.00 lakh on a test whose result he read backwards, and had learned that his binding constraint was not money but clinics.

The answer to their shared question is not a technique but a chain of arithmetic: from the decision's economics to a threshold, to a measurable quantity, to a sample design, to a price. Their numbers run through this page, because the argument is not that experiments are good but that most so-called discovery experiments are not.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A discovery experiment is a bounded act, taken before a product is built, whose purpose is to create a chance that a named belief will be shown false. Bounded: fixed cost and end date. Named: one proposition, with a who, a what, a how many and a by when. False: the design must admit a result that stops the plan, written down beforehand. A test that cannot fail is a demonstration, and demonstrations always succeed.

The older line is about inference: what can be concluded, with what uncertainty, from a design of a given size. The younger is about velocity. The practice exists because software teams can build almost anything, so the discovery that a plan was wrong migrated to the project's end. Four schools disagree about how to move it back.

The fourth school is least taught and most useful, because it supplies what the slogan lacks. “The cheapest test that could prove this wrong” is a heuristic for a calculation: maximise the value of what you learn, less what you pay in money and delay. What follows works that calculation.

3. Mechanics: the chain from economics to design

And information is worth most when the decision is close: EVPI peaks at the indifference prior, 63.15/98.00 = 0.644, at ₹22.46 lakh, and collapses at both ends. A team already sure should not be testing.

Lochan's version explains why money was never his constraint. Over three years, 120 clinics at 180 enrolled patients each give 86,400 patient-quarters a year; at ₹34 a point, a six-point overshoot of break-even is worth ₹176.26 lakh a year, so the good state nets 3×176.26 − 210.00 = +₹318.77 lakh and a six-point shortfall −₹738.77 lakh. Step six: pre-register the read

This step costs nothing, which is why it is skipped. Before the test runs, write down the number, the reader, the date, the action each range triggers, and who may overrule it. Without it the result is read in the same meeting as the roadmap, and 5 per cent is “a promising signal” or “a clear no” according to what else is on the agenda.

4. The conditions, stated as claims that can fail

C1. The decision is open, and the result could close it either way. True for Lavina; partly false for Lochan, whose pilot clinics are exclusive for twelve months, so design D forecloses 70 of them whatever the outcome. C2. The population observed is drawn from the population to be served. False for the painted door, and falser than it looks for Lavina: Tier A is her best-fit tier. C3. The observed behaviour costs the subject something in the currency the real behaviour will cost. A ₹2 lakh deposit qualifies; a “notify me” tap does not, and the difference is not one of degree. C4. The test does not consume the asset it tests. Clinics, goodwill and brand permission are consumable, and a failed pilot has spent them. C5. The delay costs less than the information is worth. Checkable against EVPI.

Three situations make the idea misleading rather than merely inapplicable. A decision insensitive to the result — a module built because a flagship renewal depends on it — has EVPI near zero, so the test is theatre. A compound assumption lets the cheapest test disprove whichever component is cheapest to disprove, which may be the one nobody cares about: “manufacturers will pay for better delivery dates” hides three separate claims. And cheapness can come from measuring something adjacent — a landing page measures the appeal of a sentence, which is evidence only if the sentence is the product.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Two-sided and marketplace. Ujas Care cannot test patient demand without clinic supply, so the clinic is both the supply side to be recruited and the cluster that destroys power. Randomising by geography to stop cross-side contamination makes it worse: cities are fewer than clinics and the design effect rises with cluster size. Mature marketplaces mostly switch to switchbacks.

Regulated. The cuff is a device under CDSCO rules; the insurer is supervised by IRDAI, so contract terms cannot be varied mid-pilot; and the DPDP Act, 2023 governs the consent under which refill data is processed, so a fake door implying clinical benefit is a compliance incident. The viability test therefore runs first and is usually cheapest — ₹2.80 lakh of counsel's time — because it rules designs out before anybody builds.

Hardware plus software. The cuff's sixteen-week tooling lead time inverts the order: a demand test that succeeds creates a commitment you cannot fulfil for four months, and one run on a borrowed cuff tests a different product. Handle it by testing demand against a service promise.

AI-native, and the cheapest test of all. Lavina's module is a prediction problem, so its feasibility risk is not “can we build it” but “what accuracy is reachable on the data we have” — answerable on data already held. Lokesh Nimkar spent eleven days and ₹1.10 lakh backtesting a date engine on 41,800 order lines from six customers, April 2025 to September 2026. The fixed nine-day buffer had delivered 29,850 of 41,800 lines by the promised date, 71.4 per cent; the best model reached 33,690 of 41,800, 80.6 per cent, against the 95 per cent his three largest accounts wanted contractually. The module could not be built to the standard it was being sold at.

The organisational seams. A pilot becomes a product because a salesperson sold it as one, so the kill criterion is now a customer commitment. A negative result lands after the roadmap was communicated and is reinterpreted. Finance books pilot revenue, after which stopping is a revenue event. Mature companies say they run disciplined assumption tests; mostly they run unstoppable pilots.

6. Four things that separate an expert

One: the threshold precedes the test and comes from the economics. Lochan's 12.0 points are ₹408 divided by the ₹34 a point that ₹3,400 buys; the ₹190 baseline cost cancels. The tell: asked what would stop them, a team produces a number suspiciously close to what they expect. An uncommitted number gets read against the organisation's appetite, not the plan's arithmetic.

Two: the cheapest disproving test is usually retrospective. Experts query the warehouse before designing anything, because historical data is paid for and carries no delay; Ujjayan's backtest cost ₹1.10 lakh against ₹6.40 lakh and reached the stronger conclusion. The tell: every test on the plan makes new data and none interrogates old. The miss is cultural — analysing existing data does not feel like discovery, so it is not counted as a test.

Three: the unit of allocation sets your power; the unit of analysis only sets your table. An expert's first question about a field test is what exactly is randomised; the second is the binomial floor check. The tell: a power calculation counting patients or order lines with no mention of clinics, accounts or warehouses. The obvious reading — that more subjects always buys power — fails once ρ > 0, because past a cluster size near 1/ρ extra subjects buy almost nothing.

Four: when the population is small and finite, stop estimating and start counting. Three signatures from eight asks gives 37.5 per cent and a 95 per cent Wilson interval of 13.7 to 69.4 per cent, which holds both disaster and triumph and straddles the 58 per cent that matters. Asking more would narrow it — eight of nineteen is already 42 per cent of the population, and a finite-population correction tightens it further — but precision is the wrong remedy, because there is no population beyond the nineteen to estimate for. Census all nineteen, count signatures against the eleven needed, and price what the census consumes.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the population is large, randomisation is cheap, and the binding risk is the base: a card placed where only engaged users see it. In business and enterprise products the population is small and finite, so sequential census with pre-sales replaces the statistical machinery, and a test conflating economic buyer and operator informs on neither. On a shared platform the treatment leaks through the common surface, so the unit of allocation must be the tenant. Hardware inverts the order, tooling having lead time. AI products admit a near-free retrospective test and punish teams that stop there.

By stage: pre-seed has no base to sample from, so it tests with money. Growth-stage has the traffic for controlled experiments and lacks the discipline to power them. Late-stage has both, and its constraint moves from inference to politics. The chain itself does not change.

9. Four failure modes, with their early warning and late cost

The unnamed denominator. Sign: a rate reported without its counts. Diagnostic: who was eligible to appear in that denominator, over the same window as the numerator? Cost late: ₹41.00 lakh committed, ₹31.88 lakh of it unrecoverable, plus a draft audit protocol that would have scored 86 of design A's 360 treated patients against short windows.

Clustering ignored. Sign: a power calculation that counts subjects and never says what was randomised. Diagnostic: what is the unit of allocation, the mean cluster size, and does the between-cluster variance clear p(1−p)/m? Cost late: a trial that cannot tell 12 points from nothing, read as a null.

The underpowered pilot read as a verdict. Sign: a design document with no minimum detectable effect. Diagnostic: what is the smallest effect it detects, and is that below what break-even needs? Cost late: ₹210.00 lakh of rollout on a false positive, or abandoning ₹176.26 lakh a year.

The unfalsifiable read. Sign: no pre-written decision rule, the result scheduled for the roadmap meeting. Diagnostic: what number, written beforehand, would make us stop, and who may overrule it? Cost late: the whole build, and the lesson that discovery is advisory.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Rigour against velocity. The controlled-experimentation position at its strongest: an underpowered test is worse than none, because it converts noise into a licence to decide; its evidence is the record of effects that reversed sign when properly powered. The pretotyping position at its strongest: the dominant error is paralysis, the alternative to a weak test is an opinion, and cheap tests aggregate faster than one expensive one. For the first to be wrong, decisions on weak evidence would have to be no worse than decisions on none — plausible when the next action is cheap and reversible. For the second, they would have to mislead in one direction, which the painted door suggests they do.

Do letters of intent mean anything? The pre-sales school: a signature with money attached is the strongest obtainable pre-build evidence, and in small-N enterprise the only kind that scales to a decision. The sceptics: an LOI is a free option, since signing costs a procurement manager nothing and deposits are refundable. Both rest on one observation, that conversion varies with what the signature cost; settling it needs the conversion rate at a given deposit size in a given segment. Lavina's ₹2 lakh is real money to a mid-market manufacturer and trivial to a conglomerate.

Can AI products be tested before they are used? One camp: offline evaluation on held-out data suffices, being cheap and reproducible. The other: only staged online exposure counts, because model behaviour interacts with user behaviour, the input distribution shifts once the product exists, and offline metrics over-predict online performance. Lokesh's backtest shows the first camp's use and the second's limit at once: decisive about a ceiling, 80.6 against 95 per cent, and worthless as a prediction of what planners would do with a band. Unresolved: whether an offline gap of known size can be corrected for.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks for the denominator before the rate, and for the window it was measured over. They refuse to design a test until the threshold has been derived from the plan's arithmetic, and they write it where others can see it. They treat what to randomise as the central design decision, and check the binomial floor before quoting an intra-cluster correlation. And they will say, in front of a sponsor, that an assumption should not be tested at all — the decision being made, or no result would change it, or the information being worth less than the delay. That last is the clearest marker: studying this makes people want to run tests; commanding it makes them run fewer.

12. What they decided

On Friday 20 November, Lavina killed the full-scope Urmi Promise and funded the narrow advisory band at ₹47.00 lakh. Two sentences carried it: the module could reach 80.6 per cent on-time against a contractual 95, so it could not be sold honestly at any price; and the demand evidence, generously recomputed, yielded 8.5 signatures and ₹119 lakh against ₹147.15 lakh. A probabilistic date with a stated confidence is a product the 80.6 per cent model can support. At ₹9 lakh a year it needs 5.22 accounts, so six. Because nineteen less thirteen refusals still leaves six, the arithmetic kill rule is toothless; her criterion is a calendar, six signatures in three weeks or stop.

On Friday 11 December, Lochan abandoned design A for design D in two stages: 36 clinics now with a 4-point futility boundary at 90 days, 70 only if it is cleared. He recorded three things before the first clinic was enrolled — that the number to beat is a 12.0-point lift, being ₹408 of incremental cost over the ₹34 a point that ₹3,400 buys, with the ₹190 baseline cost cancelling between the columns; that the design detects 13.4 points, so a true effect between 12.0 and 13.4 may be missed and that is an accepted risk; and that the audit window runs 90 days from each patient's enrolment and nothing else.

  1. Lavina's ₹6.40 lakh demand test ran before Lokesh's ₹1.10 lakh backtest. What made that order feel natural, and what rule would change it without making Ujjayan slower?
  2. Lochan accepts an 11.3 per cent chance of abandoning a programme worth ₹176.26 lakh a year to release 34 clinics and a quarter. Is that defensible, and what would you need to know to argue otherwise?
  3. The painted door measured real behaviour and was still wrong by a factor of 4.2. Had the base been correct, would a 4.1 per cent tap rate have justified ₹210.00 lakh? If not, what was it for?

13. Going deeper

The four product risks is the prerequisite taxonomy; the evidence ladder formalises figure 2's strength axis. Landing-page and smoke tests and fake doors and painted doors are the cheap rungs; 8(c) is how they fail. Concierge and Wizard of Oz tests buy behavioural evidence by hand, arguably where Ujas Care should have begun; prototype testing covers the usability risk no test here touches; pre-sales, LOIs and deposits is Lavina's instrument. Kill criteria and decision rules makes step six rigorous; dual-track discovery and delivery makes the chain a habit; pilots and beta programmes and designing enterprise pilots that convert matter because the pilot consumes its subject. Running a discovery experiment portfolio generalises the EVPI table to a budget; false positives in discovery formalises the painted door's error. Feasibility spikes and validating hardware concepts before tooling cover the ordering lead times force; discovery for AI products extends the backtest online; viability checks: legal, finance, brand, ops and validation under regulatory constraint explain why here the cheapest disproving test was a lawyer.
